## G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T

- A model was developed for detecting soil temperature and soil moisture dynamics in solar farms.

- Soil moisture content was increased by 59.8% to 113.6% in the Middle and Front zones.

- Soil temperature was decreased by 1.47 to 1.66 °C in the intermittent shade.

- Hydrological and biogeochemical processes in solar-farm management should be better studied.

Photovoltaic technology plays an important role in the sustainable development of clean energy, and arid areas are particularly ideal locations to build large-scale solar farms, all over the world. Modifications to the energy balance and water availability through the installation of large-scale solar farms, however, fundamentally affect the energy budget, water, and biogeochemical cycles. In-situ field observations, though, fail to draw definitive conclusions on how photovoltaic panels (PVs) affect the ambient environment, or how microclimates and soil moisture evolve under the long-term, continuous, cumulative influence of PVs. Here, we designed a synthetic model, integrating processes of energy budget and water cycle, to quantify the ecohydrological effects of PVs on soil microclimate and moisture regimes at different locations (zones) near individual PVs. Simulations run with a stochastically generated 100-year climate time series were examined to capture the evolutionary trends of soil microclimate and soil moisture. The results indicate that soil moisture content was increased by 59.8% to 113.6% in the Middle and Front zones, and soil temperature was decreased by 1.47 to 1.66 °C in all the sheltered zones, mainly because there was 5– 7 times more available water and ~27% less available radiation there, compared with the control zone. On the other hand, if the ground clearance of the PVs is too low, turbulence beneath hot PVs will have a significant influence on not only soil temperature but also soil moisture content. The innovative contribution of this study lies in reinforcing existing theoretical patterns for the development of soil microclimate and moisture dynamics influenced by PVs, and can be used to provide reliable insights into the hydrological and biogeochemical processes on Earth and the sustainable management of large-scale solar farms in arid ecosystems.

## 1. Introduction

Growing environmental concerns and the increasing demand for energy are opening up new opportunities for the utilization of renewable energy resources. As one of the most promising candidates for lowcarbon, non-fossil fuel energy production, solar photovoltaic (PV) technology is believed to have potential for shaping a clean, reliable, scalable and affordable electricity system for the future (Hosenuzzaman et al., 2015; Qerimi et al., 2020). According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), the total installed capacity of solar power had reached 714 GW by 2020, and the growth rate of solar power generation continues to accelerate (IRENA, 2021). Arid and semiarid regions cover more than 40% of Earth's terrestrial surface (Liu et al., 2020a). These lands are of great interest for PV applications due to their high solar potential (Tanner et al., 2020): the climatic conditions can provide high rates of solar irradiation throughout the year, and the abundant land resources can support large solar-power generating stations (Adeh et al., 2019). However, these regions, because of their stressful conditions and sparse vegetation, are fragile and sensitive ecological environments and are vulnerable to any human activities that could exacerbate the stresses they are subjected to (Hassanpour Adeh et al., 2018; Yue et al., 2021). Thus, while establishing that solar PVs would clearly provide environmental benefits by reducing carbon emissions, it is obvious that these systems could also create new environmental problems—in other words, threats as well as untapped benefits. For instance, more vigorously growing vegetation has been frequently reported in solar farms established in dry climates (the biomass has sometimes increased by 22.7 times compared with their surrounding regions), due to the shading effects of the solar panels, which resemble natural ecotones that tend to generate greater plant coverage and biomass (Bousselot et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019). Through significantly altering the water/energy availability, and thereby the interaction modes between soil and air, the expansion of ground-mounted solar farms might further affect soil carbon cycling and promote the growth of plants that can absorb greenhouse gas emissions (Jahanfar et al., 2019; Tanner et al., 2020; Thorne et al., 2015). Yet not enough is known about these effects.

Microclimates are known to influence the nature of local soil and its relationship with plants (Armstrong et al., 2014). Large-scale solar farms may incur unintended ecohydrological effects through modifications of the energy budget and water cycle (Bousselot et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019), and thus change the temperature and moisture conditions of the surface soil (Armstrong et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2018). Indeed, the changed microclimate can have various and even opposing effects on the “under-PV” environment, depending on the climate, soil, vegetation, and PV system configuration (i.e., ground clearance, tilt angle, and PV materials) (Armstrong et al., 2016; Elamri et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Onyshchenko et al., 2020). For example, besides transforming a substantial portion of incoming radiation into electricity, PVs also reflect and re-radiate solar radiation and cast heavy shade on the ground, thereby lowering soil temperatures and consequently reducing the rate of thermal-induced loss of water from soil underneath the PVs (surface soil evaporation) (Armstrong et al., 2016; Tanner et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2021). Conversely, however, PVs have low albedo and heat capacity, so that the air beneath the PVs may be heated more rapidly than in the open areas, resulting in potentially higher air temperature, lower relative humidity, and thus increased evapotranspiration water loss by both the soil and plants (Wu et al., 2014). Moreover, shifts in rainfall patterns caused by PV panels change the water inputs to the soil, resulting in both increased and reduced spatial water availability (Jahanfar et al., 2019; Tanner et al., 2020). Changes in wind patterns alter site-specific air-current regimes and evoke substantial changes in microclimates occurring over short distances as well. The abovementioned complex effects of PVs on microclimate may in turn substantially affect local vegetation structure, biodiversity and carbon balance, resulting in changes in ecosystem services at multiple scales (Bousselot et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019).

Since solar farms may potentially affect the patterns of local and even regional ecosystems through changed microclimates (Yang et al., 2018; Yue et al., 2021), these related ecological and environmental issues are becoming a matter of public and governmental concern, including whether solar farms suck up all the energy from the sun or become a photovoltaic heat island, and thus prevent plants from growing in the vicinity of the PV panels (Fthenakis and Yu, 2013; Zhe et al., 2019); whether solar farms can lead to greater ecological diversity when compared with equivalent undeveloped sites (Tanner et al., 2020); and so on (Montag et al., 2016). This is especially the case in arid and semiarid regions like northwestern China, where the climate is dry, ecosystems are being degraded, and solar farms are booming (Liu et al. (2019). Improved understanding of soil microclimate and moisture regimes is urgently needed to respond to these concerns, but only a few studies have been done so far on the ecohydrological effects of PVs for this region or other similar regions around the world (Nash et al., 2016; Yue et al., 2021). The available insitu observations have suggested that PV panels reduce the available irradiance (Araki et al., 2017), lower the soil temperature (Armstrong et al., 2016), or elevate soil moisture content, at local scales (Yue et al., 2021). However, the existing measurements at PV-plant level and regional scales have disclosed that either heat- or cold-island effects could be found, depending on the scale of observation (Gao et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020). It is clear that PVs' effects on the local climate and how these in turn impact the vegetation and soil are still not certain. Due to the inherent limitation of field observation, a synthetic modeling approach is the only possible way to bridge the gap between observations at different sites and scales, but this type of research is still lacking to date (Elamri et al., 2018; Scherba et al., 2011). There are two major difficulties in developing such a model: 1) potential applicability for the varieties of solar farms in terms of climate, configuration and location, and 2) spatially explicit descriptions of the PV-affected ecohydrological processes (Nemet, 2009; Yang et al., 2018).

Here we designed a synthetic model based on field observations, with daily timestep, to quantify the ecohydrological effects of PVs on soil microclimate and moisture regimes for different ground zones in relation to PVs. The salient advantage of our model over existing models is the spatially explicit treatment of the processes of energy budget and the water cycle, which overcame the limitations involved in evaluating the ecohydrological effects of photovoltaic solar farms using limited field observations. Through modeling efforts, this work aimed 1) to explore the ecohydrological effects of PVs on soil microclimates and moisture regimes by using a synthetic model; 2) to provide a quantitative comprehension of how PVs affect the ambient environment, or how microclimates and soil moisture evolve under the long-term, continuous, cumulative influence of PVs; and 3) to identify the moisture regimes that may further affect the carbon cycle. In order to achieve these aims, a set of numerical experiments was designed, to provide a solid basis for understanding the ecohydrological processes of large-scale solar farms in an arid ecosystem over a stochastically generated 100year climate time series, which is long enough to reasonably capture the evolutionary trends of soil microclimate and soil moisture.

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Site description and field data collection

This study was carried out at a solar farm (38°06'8"N, 102°19'47"E; 1702 m a.s.l.) located in the town of Wuwei in Gansu Province, in the eastern part of the Hexi Corridor in arid northwest China. This area has a typical temperate continental arid climate with an annual average temperature of 14.2 °C (maximum daily temperature of 35.3 °C and minimum daily temperature of -10.9 °C). The average annual precipitation is approximately 212 mm with 88% occurring during the growing season (from April 1 to September 30) based on the last 38 years of available meteorological records (1980-2017 inclusive). Just as for other arid and semiarid areas, the soil moisture content in the study

site is low, due to strong evapotranspiration, sterile soil and high-albedo surfaces, creating a harsh growing environment for vegetation (Liu et al., 2020a, 2020b). A large number of photovoltaic solar farms and concentrated solar plants have been built in this area. At the study site, the PVs are arranged in east–west orientated rows and inclined southward at a tilt angle of 37.5°, and the length and width of a single photovoltaic panel (which consists of two sub-panels with a 3-cm gap between them) are 4 m and 1 m, respectively. The underlying surface is typical of the Gobi Desert, and the soil contains gravel of varying sizes (Fig. 1c), making it difficult to install a time domain reflectometer (TDR). In order to facilitate the installation of TDR (Fig. 1a), the existing top 1 m of soil was replaced with sandy loam.

The meteorological data from 1980 to 2017 (daily maximum and minimum air temperature, sunshine duration, and total precipitation), ob— served at the Yongchang site which is about 30 km away from the solar — farm (Fig. 2a) were obtained from the National Meteorological Science Data Center, China. The volumetric moisture content (VWC) was taken to be the average of vertical profiles where the probes were installed at five depths below the soil surface (10, 20, 40, 60, and 80 cm) in each plot, and data were collected at 10-min scan intervals. The soil moisture and soil temperature were measured at each point by the TDR probes (ECH2O, Decagon Devices, Inc.). Because of the high rainfall and solar radiation availability differences among experimental zones caused by the PVs, four experimental zones were set up in order to describe the variability of soil moisture at different positions in relation to the PVs (Fig. 1a): Front (rainfall interception zone), Middle (rainfall interception and shade zone), Back (shade zone), and Control (natural bare zone). The reference monitoring site (Control) was located in an open space approximately 100 m away from the PVs, so that it was not covered by PVs.

## 2.2. Model structures and simulation methods

The scheme of the synthetic model is shown in Fig. 2b. The edge effect is not considered in the model. The aim was to assess the long-term

effects of large-scale solar farms on moisture regimes and soil microclimates. A single-site daily stochastic weather generation model (WeaGet) (Chen et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2012)—a Richardsonbased weather generator (Richardson, 1981)—was used to generate rainfall, maximum and minimum air temperature, and solar radiation over a 100-year period, as the inputs of the residual submodules. In the WeaGet, a first-order two-state Markov chain was used to generate the occurrence of wet or dry days. The probability of precipitation on a given day is based on the wet or dry status of the previous day with a two-parameter gamma distribution for precipitation amounts. We assume that rainfall is an instantaneous process because the duration of each rainfall event is short relative to the daily scale. One first-order linear autoregressive model was used to generate maximum and minimum air temperatures (Tmax and Tmin) and solar radiation at a daily scale. To obtain the most suitable soil parameters, a range of possible values of soil parameters were obtained from the literature (Laio et al., 2001b; Liu et al., 2020a, 2020b) and calibrated by in-situ observation results using the genetic algorithm method, and statistical analysis was employed to evaluate the performance of the parameters. Numerical experiments with different restrictive treatments were then designed to quantify the ecohydrological effects of PVs on soil microclimate and moisture regimes at different locations (zones) near individual PVs. The model structures are detailed as below and in Appendixes A and B.

## 2.2.3. Shading effects

The available solar radiation of the area beneath the PVs has been reduced because the PVs are intercepting a portion of the solar radiation. This shading effect has an influence on not only PET but also air and soil temperature. The amount of radiation beneath the PVs depends on the reflectivity and electricity transform efficiency of the PVs. In order to simplify the model, the shade effect of the PVs was not calculated by the mechanism model specifically. Rather, we assumed the reflectivity and electricity transform efficiency to be 10% and 18%, respectively, as those are the global average levels (Hu et al., 2016). Therefore, the residual (90%) can be divided into 18% (of the remaining 90%) absorbed by the PVs and converted to electricity, and the other 82% (of the remaining 90%) transmitted through the panels and absorbed by the underlying surface. Thus, the available solar radiation underneath the PVs is equal to 73.8% (90% × 82%) of the incoming solar radiation on the surface of the PVs.

## 2.2.4. Rain redistribution effects

When rainfall occurs, the PVs intercept some of it, and most of the intercepted rainfall flows down to the edge of the PVs and drips down forming a narrow drip line (Fig. 1b and c). After the vegetation intercepts a small portion of the dripped water, the residual will infiltrate downward through pores of soil or generate Hortonian overland flow, depending on the rainfall intensity. When the soil reaches its field capacity (i.e., the volume of water able to be retained in the soil against gravity drainage), deep drainage occurs and begins to dominate the water losses from soil. This process is explicitly described by Jahanfar et al. (2019). In more detail and more specifically, the impervious surface of the solar panels produces a roof effect that delineates a sheltered area (Fig. 1a).

Rainfall usually does not vertically drip onto the surface of the ground, as it is under the effect of the velocity of wind and raindrops. Instead, it arrives at the ground with the incidence angle (α) of rainfall with respect to the vertical direction. The model adopted to estimate

the intercepted rainfall by the PVs is the AVrain model (Agrivoltaic Plot Rain Redistribution Model) proposed by Elamri et al. (2018). For the sake of simplicity, the model assumes the irregular flow of water above the PVs is homogeneous downward flow, and the output rainfall concentrates on an area of 0.15 m width covering the edge of the PVs. ## 3. Results

## 3.1. Model validation and evaluation metrics

Parameter calibration was carried out for the Front zone, where the magnitudes of soil moisture pulses are of the most concern to us. Meanwhile, the change of meteorological elements in the Front zone is relatively simple: only water availability changed. The simulated soil depth at the site is about 80 cm where groundwater does not have active impacts on the soil moisture. The soil porosity (n) and field capacity (Sfc) were estimated as 0.41 and 0.21, respectively. The corresponding values of SW and S[⁎] were estimated as 0.09 and 0.16, respectively. Other parameters are given in Table 1, and these soil physical parameters are within the reasonable range of the values reported in the literature for sandy loam. Different values of KC were adopted for the early growing season (from Apr 1rd to Jun 30rd) and late growing season (from Jul 1rd to Sep 30rd), as the evapotranspiration rate is related to the leaf area. The observed and simulated processes of soil responding to the rainfall and the soil-drying process at the four different zones for the year 2016 are shown in Fig. 3a, and there was no significant difference between the observed and simulated values in the Front zone, with NSE = 0.68 and RMSE of the observed and simulated soil moisture content of the Middle zone equal to 0.02 v/v. The simulated average soil temperature calculated by Eq. (1) (Fig. 3b) is similar to the observed value, with RMSE = 2.45 v/v. The average soil temperature appears to have been slightly underestimated in the summer. But since Eq. (1) successfully simulates the trend of soil temperature, the errors generated by the model are within acceptable limits.

## 3.2. Soil microclimate features affected by the PVs

In order to avoid uncertainties attributable to the initial start-up operation of the solar farm, the model was run for a study period of — 100 years by which time the meteorological and soil microclimate elements in the solar farm would have stabilized enough to capture climatic fluctuations—to study the difference in soil temperature between the PV-sheltered zone and natural bare soil. Annual average soil temperature in the sheltered zone is 1.47– 1.66 °C lower than in the natural bare soil (Fig. 4). Meanwhile, the soil temperature does not show strong variability, for either the sheltered zone or the control; the corresponding values of the coefficient of variation are equal to 0.0032 and 0.0039, respectively. Although the reduction of surface radiation is a long-term, continuous, cumulative process, the simulated results indicate that soil temperature beneath the PVs is not gradually becoming cooler, but is rather relatively stable, with normal fluctuations. Furthermore, no obvious difference in probability of daily average soil temperature was found (Fig. 4b), although the probability was that daily average soil temperature in the sheltered zone is in the range of 25 to 32 °C— higher than in the control; this difference might be attributed to the warming effect of PVs because of their low albedo and heat capacity. In general, the control zone was warmer than the sheltered zone. This phenomenon will be discussed in Section 4.2.

## 3.3. Soil moisture regimes affected by the PVs

The average annual soil moisture in the rainfall interception zones, for the Front and Middle zones, were 16.3% and 15.8%, respectively, about twice as high as in the Control zone, where it was only 8%

(Fig. 5a). Soil moisture content of the rainfall interception zones was distributed in a range of 7% to 20%. However, the values in the Control zone only varied from 6% to 13% (Fig. 5b), and the number of days when soil moisture content was less than the wilting point came to about 72% of the growing season. Compared with the Control, the water stress tended to be more severe in the Back zone (Fig. 5). Since lower soil moisture content is usually accompanied by lower soil moisture variability, this result simply and intuitively reflects the influence of PVs on the soil moisture dynamics. During the 100-year time series, soil moisture variability in the rainfall interception zones was higher than in - the Control or Back zones, with the corresponding values of the coeffi cient of variation equaling 0.24, 0.22, 0.12, and 0.09, respectively. There is an obvious soil moisture content gradient: the highest soil moisture is located at the Front and the lowest at the Back instead of the Control. In general, the areas beneath the PVs were wetter, and the PVs could raise the local soil moisture content by 59.8% to 113.6%.

## 4.2. How do PVs change the soil microclimate features?

Less net radiation compared with natural bare soil leads to lower soil temperature, as was proved in our simulated results (Fig. 4) and by the observed results reported in the literature (Jahanfar et al., 2016; Suuronen et al., 2017; Tanner et al., 2014). In this context, one concern is whether a large-scale solar farm, usually built in a short time, will rapidly and significantly modify soil temperature, and cause a “cool island” effect that makes the soil beneath the PVs become cooler and cooler over time. However, this concern was not confirmed by the simulated results in this work. From an energy-balance point of view, the net radiation the soil accepts can be divided into three components: latent heat flux between the soil and the atmosphere, sensible heat flux between upper and lower soil boundaries, and soil sensible heat storage which directly controls soil temperature (Heitman et al., 2008a; Heitman et al., 2008b). The latter two mainly depend on the thermodynamic properties of the soil (Seneviratne et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2001). Therefore, soil temperature is mainly influenced by available net radiation, evapotranspiration rate, and soil thermodynamic properties. These are also the ways in which PVs most likely affect soil temperature. In theory, whether the net radiation beneath PVs rises or falls depends on the albedo difference between the PVs and the natural land surface. In arid desert areas, the amount of net radiation tends to be reduced because PVs reflect a portion of the incoming radiation to the atmosphere and convert a small amount (~20%) of residual energy into electricity (Barron-Gafford et al., 2016).

Coupled energy and water exchange processes occurring in the land-atmosphere boundary are principally linked by evapotranspiration, which is an expenditure of both energy and soil moisture (Brubaker and Entekhabi, 1996; Heitman et al., 2008a). As a result, evapotranspiration intensity and soil temperature tend to be positively correlated. In a warm/dry anomaly, elevated temperature will stimulate increased evaporation in order to cool the surface, and vice versa

(Brubaker and Entekhabi, 1996). Therefore, PVs can change evaporation or evapotranspiration intensity to influence soil temperature. Furthermore, soil volumetric heat capacity is also one of the controlling factors of soil temperature. It is affected by all three components — air, liquid, and soil (Sakai et al., 2011). As the effect of air on soil volumetric heat capacity is usually ignored, soil volumetric heat capacity depends mainly on soil water content and solid components. Although there have been no reports that PVs obviously change soil physicochemical properties, PVs can change the spatial distribution of rainfall and increase soil moisture at their edges (Fig. 5). Higher soil water content will increase the amount of heat required for the soil temperature to rise, which benefits soil by maintaining a relatively lower temperature compared with dry soil.

## 4.3. How do PVs control the moisture regimes beneath them?

In an arid environment, PVs’ roof effect increases water availability (Hernandez et al., 2020), which is a restrictive environmental factor for the survival of vegetation, insects, and small animals (Jacobs et al., 2000, P.Mckay et al., 2003), and affects the moisture regimes beneath the PVs (P.Mckay et al., 2003, Vale and Brito, 2015). Although observed results can provide clarity and reinforce intuitive expectations of soil moisture regimes affected by PVs, the mechanisms of how PVs influence soil moisture regimes are still not revealed through short-term observation alone. As is well known, the evapotranspiration rate depends on soil moisture content and energy availability. As mentioned in Section 4.2, there is a negative relationship between soil moisture and evapotranspiration rate (Brubaker and Entekhabi, 1996); hence, changes in evapotranspiration intensity caused by PVs also have an effect on soil moisture regimes. Because there are so many confounding factors, predictions of the effects of PVs are best conducted using ecological models (Nouvellon et al., 2000). Different restrictive treatments are input to the model (Fig. 6), with the aim of providing a comprehensive quantitative view of how PVs influence soil moisture regimes through their effects on coupled energy and water processes occurring at the land-atmosphere boundary.

We assumed that PVs do not intercept natural precipitation or change the spatial distribution of precipitation; they only shade the surface beneath them (Fig. 6a). The simulated soil moisture results from this shading effect were about 33%–44% lower than the observed results in the Middle and Front zones, showing that the roof effect does have a significant influence on soil moisture content. As discussed in Section 4.1, available radiation has a significant influence on soil mois- ture, so we compared the effects of different radiation interception effi ciencies on soil moisture (Figs. 3 and 6b). NSE decreased from -0.8 to -3, and annual average soil moisture increased from 0.15 to 0.18 when available solar radiation decreased 20% in the sheltered zone. These results indicate that there is a negative correlation between available radiation and soil moisture, a result consistent with previous conclusions about the effects of available radiation on soil moisture.

Even when solar radiation was correctly estimated, the simulation of soil moisture dynamics in the Middle zone still did not fit well with the observations, with NSE = -2 (Fig. 6c), because evapotranspiration in the Middle zone was underestimated. The surface temperature of a PV is usually ~20 °C higher than the nearby air temperature (Fthenakis and Yu, 2013)—a temperature so hot that the PV will re-radiate the energy as longwave radiation, and the air beneath the PV will be heated by the PV itself. Consequent wind velocity reduction has been reported in the literature (Yuan et al., 2016). Such hot and low-velocity turbulence might have a strong influence on evapotranspiration. In other words, the higher air temperature and lower wind velocity under PVs (as in the Middle zone here) can cause evaporation intensity to be significantly stronger than in other zones. In order to reflect the effect of air turbulence on soil moisture regime, the daily maximum temperature was increased by 50% in the simulation (Fig. 3a). Although the Middle zone has the same water availability as the Front, and less radiation, soil moisture in the Middle was even lower than in the Front because turbulence increases evapotranspiration intensity (Fig. 3a). The result indicates that turbulence has a significant effect on soil moisture. Yet there is another uncertain factor that might have an even stronger influence on soil moisture regime: the PVs’ rainfall harvesting efficiency. In the model, we assumed that water flow on the PVs’ surfaces is homogeneous without redistribution, but this assumption is not true. Water might flow out of the longitudinal slit, or through the cross gap between the two sub-panels when the intensity of the rain is above a certain - threshold. In order to test that conjecture, the rainfall harvesting effi ciencies in the Front and Middle zones were set to 0.8 and 0.65, respectively (Fig. 6d), enabling the model to capture the magnitudes of soil moisture pulses and the shapes of the soil-drying process better than is indicated in Fig. 3a, with NSE equal to 0.67 and 0.13, respectively. In a word, PVs affect the soil moisture regime mainly through changing available radiation and water. Furthermore, turbulence and rainfall in homogeneous flow might also have a significant influence on the soil moisture regimes.

## 4.4. Broad application and implications

Precipitation promotes germination and supplies food and water for vegetation and animals, especially in arid environments, and a change in water availability might have even more dramatic impacts on biodiversity compared with other ecosystems (Vale and Brito, 2015). Largescale solar farms might provide another way to mitigate water restriction in arid environments, as one 50 MWp solar farm can collect about 23,000 m[3] water per year due to the PVs’ roof effect in extremely arid zones where the average annual precipitation is less than 100 mm. Intermingling solar panels with agriculture is known as an agrivoltaic system (Brown, 2018), and these systems have been widely studied in large-scale solar farms (Adeh et al., 2019; Cossu et al., 2014; Marrou et al., 2013). Application of agrivoltaic systems in an arid environment tends to improve land utilization, rainfall use efficiency, and crop yields (Amaducci et al., 2018; Ravi et al., 2016), because the intermittent shade provided by PVs is better for crops where microclimates are more

moderate (as discussed above), and the stronger evapotranspiration is balanced by the additional precipitation intercepted by the PVs (Adeh et al., 2019). Maize (Amaducci et al., 2018), aloe vera (Ravi et al., 2016), Goji berries (Wu et al., 2014), and other crops (Adeh et al., 2019) have been studied in agrivoltaic systems. Besides the agrivoltaic — systems, other solar photovoltaic types including aquavoltaics (the combination of PVs with aquaculture), floatovoltaics (floating solar PVs on open water), and building-attached or -integrated PVs—have been widely deployed, not only sparing land needed for the installation of solar farms, but also reducing evaporation losses substantially, providing vital water savings for drought-stricken areas (Cagle et al., 2020). These PV systems, when operating in conjunction with other traditional electricity sources (e.g., floatovoltaics with hydropower), can further improve energy efficiency and reduce external evaporation (Kuriqi et al., 2021; Kuriqi et al., 2020).

In contrast to the booming development of PV power systems (Exley et al., 2021), few researches have been conducted on their ecohydrological effects on their surrounding environments. The effects of large-scale solar farms on the ecological environment have been studied mostly at the local scale, but whether large-scale solar farms will change atmospheric circulation and whether they will mitigate or intensify global warming as a result of their modification of land surface properties (e.g., surface albedo, roughness) is still not known (Hu et al., 2016; Millstein and Menon, 2011; Nemet, 2009; Yang et al., 2018). The carbon sequestration potential of a large-scale solar farm is also important to research, as solar farms are clearly beneficial for vegetation restoration, as this study has found. As for a holistic view of solar farms; although they are not free of non-renewable resource use because their manufacturing process consumes considerable non-renewable energy and materials, they are still much cleaner and have lower carbon emissions compared with coal-based or other fossil-fuel energy sources. For example, Ye et al. (2021) pointed out that over 90% of carbon emissions can be avoided with solar energy, compared with fossil-based energy. However, these researches have usually concentrated on the benefits of solar farms that have been substituted for fossil-based energy, and fail to consider the additional carbon emission reductions caused by the changes solar farms make to the ecosystem. Furthermore, the ecohydrological effects of large-scale solar farms may be different, or even contrary, when comparing daily, seasonal or interannual scales, or site, regional, or continental scales. Therefore, studies should also be conducted, on how scale can impact the ecohydrological effects of large-scale solar farms.

## 5. Conclusions

Soil microclimates and moisture regimes affected by PVs were analyzed using a synthetic model. Our study provides a solid basis for understanding the ecohydrological effects of large-scale solar farms on an arid ecosystem, and can also provide evidence to support previously observed results and maximize the ecosystem services of large-scale solar farms in arid areas. The results indicate that PVs can improve soil moisture content in the middle and front zones, by about 59.8% to 113.6%, and that an obvious soil moisture gradient exists in solar farms where the highest soil moisture is located at the front zone and the lowest at the back. Average soil temperature beneath PVs is about 1.47– 1.66 °C lower than on the ground outside the PVs, but there was no evidence that the soil becomes continuously cooler and wetter; in fact, it may be that PVs have the opposite effect on soil temperature and moisture at night, reversing the daytime effect (Armstrong et al., 2016). Turbulence associated with the ground clearance of PVs also has an influence on soil temperature and soil moisture content. In the future, agrivoltaic systems should be studied, and the sites and installation methods for solar farms should be carefully selected to avoid some of the adverse effects. Furthermore, more work is needed, to evaluate the carbon sequestration capabilities of solar farms, taking into account how they can change ecosystems, and to better understand how scale

impacts the ecohydrological effects of large solar farms. In general, however, the simulation results of this study indicate that large-scale solar farms benefit arid environments, as they can mitigate heat and water stress in arid areas and facilitate vegetation restoration.
